title: Moon Phase Calendar Map: A Month of Moons
description: View approximate daily moon phases for a selected month using a mean-cycle model.
summary_sentence: Phase labels and illumination are estimates at noon UTC and can differ from a precise local ephemeris.
quick_answer: This calendar estimates phase names and illumination at noon UTC using a fixed mean synodic cycle. It is an approximation, not a precise ephemeris or a map of moon visibility.

body.t: Star parties and meteor nights want the new-moon weekends. The grid finds them months ahead — then the
Moonrise-over-the-city shots, full-moon hikes and night markets all need the full date early. The grid is how organisers stop being surprised by their own event.

Lunar months begin at the crescent; Ramadan, Passover and lunar new years all anchor to this cycle. The calendar shows the astronomy underneath the observance — visibility of a first crescent depends on age and place, and the grid gives the age.
A printed month of Moons on the classroom wall teaches the cycle better than any diagram — students watch the lit side grow, flip and shrink across real dates they lived through.
Each calendar cell shows a phase label and estimated illumination at noon UTC. That instant may not correspond to your local evening.
For precise phase instants or local moonrise, consult a reliable astronomical ephemeris or observatory.

faq: Why can the full-moon date differ from my wall calendar?
The model uses a fixed mean cycle at noon UTC, rather than an exact lunar ephemeris. Both model error and time-zone differences can change a date.
Some months have no full moon — really?
February can: with 28 days and a 29.53-day cycle, a February roughly once in two decades holds no full moon (last in 2018). The grid shows the two fulls crowding into January and March instead.
Does the grid work for past centuries?
The year control supports 1950–2100. The mean-cycle approximation is not suitable as a precise historical ephemeris.
Can I see illumination for a whole season?
Chain the months — the pattern repeats every 19 years almost exactly (the Metonic cycle), which is why Easter tables and this calendar are cousins.
Why noon UTC for each date?
A single evaluation instant keeps dates comparable worldwide. Evenings near a phase boundary belong to the neighbouring cell in some timezones — the model says so rather than hiding it.
The phases and percents are global; the icons' lit side mirrors below the equator. The calendar's numbers travel; its pictures wear a northern accent.
How do I find the darkest weekend quickly?
Scan for the new-moon cell and take the Friday-to-Sunday around it — then check the Moon Position Map for whether even the crescent is up late.
